1	# grow_with_claudinite
2	
3	Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
4	lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
5	Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
6	existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.
7	
8	This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
9	lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
10	**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
11	that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.
12	
13	Its scheduled work is four tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
14	scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:
15	
16	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window, or a log is past retention | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI, plus the prune on the logs branch |
19	| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | weekly, when the canon or the project's local packs moved in the week | a PR against the repo's `main` |
20	| `growth-discover-packs` ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) | weekly | a new **local** pack in the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`, via a reviewed PR |
21	| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | weekly (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
22	
23	(Plus [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md), the agentless daily fold described below.)
24	
25	## Extraction is one task over two sources
26	
27	`growth-extract` is the whole capture stage, and it runs **three skills** in order:
28	
29	1. [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) over the window's commits, merged
30	   PRs and issue discussion;
31	2. [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) over the logs captured
32	   from working sessions (plus the retention prune);
33	3. [prose-to-checks](skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) over the prose **that run just wrote**, to see
34	   whether any of it upgrades to a check before the PR opens.
35	
36	Everything lands in **one** PR, delivered to land where the repo's delivery settings allow
37	(`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`). The two extraction halves used to be two tasks firing in
38	the same nightly slot against the same local packs; they share the lesson bar, the promotion ladder
39	and the dedup surface ([extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)), so the split bought nothing
40	and cost a second opus dispatch, a second PR, and two runs deduping against a corpus the other was
41	concurrently writing.
42	
43	The third step is why the standing `prose-to-checks-sweep` is **weekly**: fresh prose is already
44	offered a conversion the night it is written, so what the sweep sees is a backlog that moves on a
45	weekly clock.
46

53	How a lesson is learned in a consuming project, lifted into the shared canon when it's portable,
54	and pruned back out of the project once the canon owns it. Two packs split it by who declares them:
55	**[grow_with_claudinite](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md)** (member-side: extract + dedup + pack

57	
58	```
59	EXTRACT   per member    → auto-merging PR against the member's main   (grow_with_claudinite)
60	PROMOTE   central, once → PR against Claudinite's main                (canon-curation)
61	DEDUP     per member    → PR against the member's main                (grow_with_claudinite)
62	```
63	
64	All three are ordinary, **independent** planner units — there is no barrier and no phase ordering.
65	Each stage reads only what is already **merged**: promote processes whatever sits on members' mains
66	when it runs, so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted **tomorrow** night (the extract PR's merge
67	shows up in the next night's local-pack signal), and reaches other members' dedup once the promote PR
68	is approved and merged. That approval was always the dominant latency, so the barrier machinery bought little;
69	if the cadence ever matters, promote can run more often (twice daily, or before and after the
70	nightly) without any design change.
71	
72	**Review gates by blast radius, not uniformly.** Promote opens a PR — it's the sole judgment gate
73	before the shared canon every repo reads, so it always needs a human eye. Dedup opens a PR too — a
74	wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson. Extract lands through an **auto-merging PR** against the
75	member's `main` — it writes only that project's own local packs, so it earns a CI gate and a PR trail
76	but not a human reviewer; auto-merge keeps the fleet's daily lesson-capture from flooding review
77	requests. (An owner-requested, in-session retrospective delivers a PR for a human to review — see
78	[extracting-lessons.md](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/extracting-lessons.md).)
79	
80	**Central execution, no plumbing.** Promote runs from the Claudinite home repo with a fleet-wide
81	token, so it reads every participating member and opens its canon PR directly here — no
82	consumer-side Action, no cross-repo PAT, no labelled-issue up-path. The planner hands its gate the
83	`fleetMembers` aggregate (which members changed, and what they declare), and the gate hands the
84	worker the changed participants as `targets`.
85	
86	**This pack's tasks need the fleet executor routine — a second routine, only in this repo.** Both
87	tasks here declare `session_scope: 'fleet'`, so the scheduler files their dispatches under
88	`ready-for-agent-fleet` rather than `ready-for-agent`, and a *distinct* CCR routine runs them: named
89	`Claudinite executor - fleet`, fired by the **`ready-for-agent-fleet`** label event, with sources =
90	this repo **and every participating member** (that cross-repo reach is the whole reason the scope is
91	split, and is exactly what must stay off an ordinary project's `self` executor). Its launcher prompt
92	is the ordinary one **plus the scope word**:
93	
94	```
95	Execute the Claudinite executor: engine/scheduler/executor.md fleet
96	```
97	
98	That last word is load-bearing and easy to lose: `resolve-dispatch.mjs` defaults an unnamed scope to
99	`self`, so a fleet routine whose prompt omits it declines every dispatch with exit `11` and changes
100	nothing. The failure is **silent and permanent** — the session stops without commenting, the
101	scheduler re-arms the issue on its next hourly pass, and the pair repeats forever, so the only
102	symptom is a `ready-for-agent-fleet` issue that keeps getting re-labeled and never runs. Nothing

105	producing anything, read the routine's prompt first.
106

108	— lives with [the growth pack's extract-from-conversations skill](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)

110	member-side method docs (extract, dedup, pack discovery, and how a project's local packs are

1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local.
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
30	
31	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
32	
33	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
34	
35	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
36	
37	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
38	
39	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
40	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases, **one file per person**, named for that person's identity. This group does **not live in this repo**: personal preferences belong to a fleet's users, so they sit in the repo this project's `preferences` setting points at (`.claudinite-checks.json` → `"preferences": { "repo": … }`), one `<email>.md` per person. Route an item of this kind to that repo's file for the user it belongs to — it never goes in the practice group, and it never comes back into the canon.
41	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
42	
43	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
44	
45	### When nothing fits
46	
47	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
48	
49	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
50	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
51	
52	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
53	
54	## Keep the write surface bounded
55	
56	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.
57

The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.

This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.

An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.

## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all

The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:

- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local.
- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).

Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.

### Dedupe against the whole corpus

Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.

## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default

A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.

**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).

## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)

Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:

1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases, **one file per person**, named for that person's identity. This group does **not live in this repo**: personal preferences belong to a fleet's users, so they sit in the repo this project's `preferences` setting points at (`.claudinite-checks.json` → `"preferences": { "repo": … }`), one `<email>.md` per person. Route an item of this kind to that repo's file for the user it belongs to — it never goes in the practice group, and it never comes back into the canon.
3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.

Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.

### When nothing fits

An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:

- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).

The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.

## Keep the write surface bounded

Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.

216	  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
217	  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
218	  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
219	  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
220	  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
221	  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
222	  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
223	  that catches it.
224	- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
225	  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
226	  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
227	  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
228	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
229	  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
230	  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
231	  exception: it commits a whole working tree and re-cuts a dated family branch; the landing itself —
232	  delivery preference, CI dispatch, arm/land/merge — is shared, in `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`.)
233	- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
234	- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
235	  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
236	  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
237	  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
238	  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
239	  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
240	  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
241	  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
242	  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
243	  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
244	  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
245	  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
246	- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
247	  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
248	  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
249	  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
250	  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
251	  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
252	  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
253	  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
254	  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
255	  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
256	  return to a paused branch, before presenting it — the owner should never have to ask "is this
257	  change still needed" (asked three times on #465 before it was volunteered).
258	- **Every `Claude_Code_Remote` call costs minutes, and a call that returns nothing has NOT failed —
259	  never re-issue it.** The whole server behaves this way, not one tool: measured over four sessions
260	  on 2026-07-29, `add_repo` ran 270–285s a call, `send_later` 117–390s, `list_triggers` 139–325s,
261	  `delete_trigger` 286–301s, `subscribe_pr_activity` 14–237s. They read like cheap registrations,
262	  so a session issues one, sits through minutes of silence, concludes it hung, and issues it again —
263	  and *the duplicate is the dominant cost*, because the first call had already succeeded:
264	  **#562 (`2026-07-29T1500Z`) — 6 `add_repo` calls, 1121s of that session's 1391s of tool
265	  wall-clock (81%)**, with `HelloWorldFlutterApp` added twice (285s + 271s); **#553
266	  (`2026-07-29T2206Z`) — the same PR check-in `send_later`d 4 times, 1107s of 2028s (55%)**; **#544
267	  (`2026-07-29T1248Z`) — `list_triggers` ×2, `delete_trigger` ×2 on one trigger id, `send_later` ×2:
268	  1854s of 2472s (75%)**, in a session whose real work was 166 tool calls. `AskUserQuestion` shares
269	  the shape — #559's session asked one question twice for 218s + 204s. So: **one call per intent,
270	  ever**, and when what you want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge on
271	  the already-green result rather than buying a notification. Budget these calls before making them:
272	  four of them is most of an hour.
273	- **Sync local `main` with `git reset --hard origin/main`, never `git pull` — this repo's session
274	  clones are shallow.** The post-merge sync step of `merge-to-main` is where it bites, and it bit
275	  five separate sessions on 2026-07-29 alone (#548, #551, #537, #559 and the session-end capture of
276	  `73a4db48`). A shallow clone has no common ancestor with the fetched remote, so `git pull` either
277	  demands an explicit strategy or reports the stale local ref as carrying unique commits it does not
278	  have — and the tempting reading, "local `main` has work the remote lacks", is wrong every time:
279	  the session's own work is already *in* `origin/main`, which is why it just merged. #537's session
280	  spent 87s across `git pull`, `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and log comparisons proving
281	  that from scratch; #559's landed on "git sees no common ancestor" the same way. Nothing of value
282	  is ever on this repo's local `main`, so the sync is unconditional: `git fetch origin main && git
283	  reset --hard origin/main`. (Portable — a promote candidate for `git-github`'s merge procedure,
284	  where "your clone may be shallow" is true of any container-hosted session.)
285	- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
286	  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
287	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
288	  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
289	  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
290	  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
291	  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
292	  the repo root.
293	- **Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy has NO carrier — baseline
294	  migrations move paths, not schemas — so it lands as a fleet-wide silent break.** Vendoring
295	  refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only; a member's `.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/pack.mjs` is
296	  the member's own content, which no converge may edit. And `migrations/` cannot help: its record
297	  is a path relocation (`aliases: [{ canonical, legacy }]`, applied by `applyFileAliases`), so it
298	  has no way to express "the field `rules` is now `worldRules`/`workRules`" or "`ruleRoutingGuidance`
299	  is now required" — exactly what #555 tightened, shipping no record because there was none to
300	  ship. The break is worse than loud: `normalizeManifest` returns `{ ...mod, rules }` with `rules`
301	  rebuilt **only** from the two scoped keys, so a legacy manifest's array is overwritten with `[]`
302	  and **that pack's checks simply stop running** — no error, the pack still loads. Measured on
303	  2026-07-30: **eleven local packs across ten of the thirteen members** had to be rewritten by
304	  hand in one session, and the members' own pack tests asserted `pack.rules` and went red on CI
305	  the moment the manifests moved. So before tightening anything a member's own file must satisfy,
306	  ask what carries it across the fleet; if the answer is "nothing", the change is not ready —
307	  accept the legacy shape in `normalizeManifest` (and say so) until a carrier exists, and never
308	  let a stale declaration degrade to *fewer checks running* rather than a failure.
309	- **A migration record is always the newest code; the engine that executes its result is the
310	  member's, and only as new as its last successful converge.** `migrations/apply.mjs` runs from a
311	  **fresh canon clone**, so every member gets today's record — but the worker that then commits and
312	  pushes it is the member's own **vendored** `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs`,
313	  frozen at whatever converge last succeeded. So a record that needs a *new engine capability* to be
314	  deliverable is a **deadlock** on any member that hasn't got it yet: the record fires, the converge
315	  fails, the mount never advances — and the engine fix that would make the record deliverable can
316	  never arrive, because the only thing that could carry it is the converge the record is breaking.
317	  Measured 2026-08-05: `sheepdog-fleet-baseline` materialized `.github/workflows/fleet-baseline.yml`,
318	  which the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may not push, and wedged `missingbulb/Sheepdog`'s every converge
319	  **twice** — the second time *after* the engine fix (#651) had merged to canon, because Sheepdog was
320	  still running the pre-fix worker. So when a record depends on engine behaviour newer than the record's
321	  own landing date, make `appliesTo` **probe the member's own mount** for that capability and stay
322	  inert until it reads back — self-healing in two cycles, no manual step on any member (#652). Probe by
323	  content, not by version: the baselining stamp covers the whole mount and says nothing about *which*
324	  engine change is in it. And fail **safe** — an unreadable or missing mount file must read as "not
325	  capable", which only ever delays that one record instead of wedging the repo.
326	- **When the owner asks why something failed, lead with the throwing call site — `file:line`, the
327	  function, and which side enforced it.** He is asking for the mechanism, not the sequence; an answer
328	  that narrates the flow correctly but never names the line reads as unanswered, and he will ask again.
329	  Measured 2026-08-05 (#649): "explain why the flow failed" → a correct stage-by-stage narrative →
330	  *"You didn't explain my question from before. What exactly threw the error?"* → `worker.mjs:429`,
331	  `execFileSync` on `git push`, refused **remote-side** on receipt → understood immediately. Three
332	  rounds and ~10 minutes for one fact that fits on one line. The local/remote half matters as much as
333	  the line: it is what says why nothing local — the commit, `migrations/apply.mjs`, the suite, the
334	  sweep — saw it coming.
335	- **This repo's fleet machinery reports success from reaching the end of the code path, not from
336	  the artifact — check the response, and alarm on the stamp.** `deliver()` in
337	  `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs` destructured only `json` from the PR-open POST and
338	  never read `status`, so a 403 (the member's *"Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
339	  requests"* setting, invisible from inside the Action) put the error body in `pr`, left
340	  `pr.node_id` undefined, skipped the auto-merge arm silently — and the run still logged
341	  `preprocessing basics/baselining: ok`. It compounds because `openMaintenancePull` reuses by open
342	  **PR**, not by branch: a cycle that pushes a branch but fails to open its PR finds nothing to
343	  reuse and mints a fresh one nightly. Measured 2026-07-29/30: **eleven of twelve consumers frozen
344	  on the 2026-07-28 canon ref, 27 orphan `claudinite/maintenance-*` branches, several repos
345	  carrying two for one day** — and every nightly run green throughout. Nothing detected it; the
346	  owner did, by feel ("I feel the situation is bad"). Two habits follow. Read the status of every
347	  API write whose result you then branch on — a body-only destructure turns a refusal into a
348	  plausible object. And judge the fleet by **members' stamps**, never by scheduler run
349	  conclusions: the stamp is the only artifact that moves when baselining actually worked, which is
350	  why a stamp-staleness alarm (#331) is the missing guard and not a nice-to-have.
351	- **A fleet task's target list is enumerated dynamically; the routine's reachable-repo grant is
352	  hand-typed UI config — they drift, and the drift completes rather than fails.** The precondition
353	  builds its member list over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` (`engine/scheduler/signals/fleet.mjs`, "the one
354	  token that can enumerate every repo the owner owns"), while the executor routine's MCP repo scope
355	  is set by hand in a UI no Action can read — so every member adopted from here on is enumerated by
356	  the precondition and invisible to the executor until someone widens the grant, and the gap only
357	  ever widens. Measured 2026-07-31 on #602: the dispatch named 12 members, the session's grant
358	  listed 10, and `growth-promote` reads members **over the API, never a checkout** — so the run
359	  would have noted two denials, proceeded, and filed a PR reading as a complete 12-member sweep.
360	  That is the worse of the two failure shapes: a routing mismatch stalls visibly (nothing happens,
361	  forever, and you notice), an unreachable target *succeeds wrongly*. So a fleet task must **fail
362	  loudly on a Context target it cannot reach** rather than proceed on a partial list, and adopting a
363	  member is not done until the routine's repo scope names it. No check can catch either half — this
364	  is routine config, not repo content.
365	- **`packs/README.md`'s check tally conflicts on every concurrent check-adding PR — recompute it,
366	  never take a side.** The hand-maintained "Hardcoded conformance checks" count is a repo-wide
367	  aggregate that each PR adding a rule must bump, so two such PRs in flight always collide there,
368	  and a branch that sat overnight collides with whatever landed meanwhile. Both sides of the
369	  conflict are stale the moment a third PR merges, so picking one — or incrementing the higher —
370	  is guessing; `packs-tests/catalog-tally.test.mjs` then goes red and the loop repeats. Derive it
371	  instead: discover the packs and count the active rules (`discoverPacks` +
372	  `run-active-pack-rules.mjs`), write that number, re-run the tally test. Measured 2026-07-31: the
373	  same tally was resolved three times in one day across two sessions (67→68 in #600, then 68→69→70
374	  twice inside #593's merge sequence).
375	  The nastier half of the same tally: a PR that **forgets** the aggregate doesn't conflict at all.
376	  #607 bumped its pack's own row in the catalog table — the *other* hand-maintained number a new
377	  rule must update — and never touched the corpus tally, so it merged clean on a suite that had run
378	  **once**, 12.5 hours earlier against a base that predated #606's own check, and left `main` red
379	  for every PR after it until #608 corrected 68 → 69 as an aside. A conflict at least stops you;
380	  the omission is silent, because a whole-tree aggregate is judged against the merged result and
381	  no branch's CI ever sees that. So a green from before `main` moved is not evidence about
382	  post-merge `main`: re-run the suite against current `main` immediately before merging a
383	  rule-adding PR, and update **both** numbers. (Portable — a promote candidate for `git-github`'s
384	  `merge-to-main`, which today says nothing about merging on a stale green.)
385	- **A worker whose cwd sits inside the tree it deletes takes every child with it — and the death
386	  arrives dressed as a legitimate outcome.** Baselining's prework runs with its cwd *inside the
387	  mount* (`.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/`), and converge step 2 `rmSync`s that
388	  whole tree before re-copying it. On Linux the worker survives on the unlinked inode and so does
389	  every child it spawns — so `check_the_world` died at `process.cwd()` with `ENOENT … uv_cwd`
390	  **before running a single check**, on every night that actually converged. Nothing looked wrong,
391	  because `escalation()` folded the crash into `checks-could-not-run` (worker.mjs:184) — a real code
392	  that reads as "this mount is too old to have checks". Net effect, fleet-wide and invisible: the
393	  conformance gate had never gated a converged tree, and every converging night burned an agent
394	  escalation on it. Caught live on a Sheepdog run, by nobody's test (#689/#691). Two habits. **Give
395	  every spawned child an explicit `cwd`** — `node([…], env, { cwd: root })` — rather than letting it
396	  inherit a directory its parent is about to delete, and resolve a root that cannot vanish underneath
397	  you (`--root`, then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then `cwd`: the order `check_the_world` and
398	  `engine/selftest.mjs` now share; the disagreement between them is the only reason selftest survived
399	  the same dead cwd untouched). And **when a crash and a benign state share one outcome code, the
400	  crash is unobservable** — keep "could not run" distinguishable from "had nothing to run".
401	- **When a member's maintenance PR won't land, read the member before theorizing — `unstable` beside
402	  a green sweep is a *parked* run, not a missing repo setting.** GitHub gates `pull_request` runs on
403	  Actions-pushed branches at `action_required`; a parked run never reports, so the PR reads
404	  `mergeable_state: unstable` and `enablePullRequestAutoMerge` refuses it. Measured 2026-08-07 (#676):
405	  a session read that signature as the members lacking *"Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve
406	  pull requests"* and offered to have the owner flip it across the fleet. The owner's *"Check that
407	  setting. I think you're wrong."* was right, and the two reads that settled it took under a minute —
408	  each member's raw `.claudinite-checks.json` (all eight already said `delivery: auto-merge`) and the
409	  head sha's `pull_request` runs (4 of the last 5 parked `action_required`). The tree already knew:
410	  `baselining/worker.mjs` documents both shapes and the session quoted the wrong one — but this is a
411	  mistake of omission you make *without* opening that file, which is why it belongs here rather than
412	  beside the code. So propose a platform-settings change only as a **conclusion**, never as a
413	  diagnosis, and never on a symptom two API reads resolve. (Sibling of the standing ruling above that
414	  what Claudinite ships must run on the settings a member already has — that one is about what to
415	  *build*, this one about what to *believe*.)
416
